To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the innate immune molecule, surfactant protein‐A (SP‐A) is present in human vaginal fluid in cyclic amounts, and that these amounts are inversely related to the levels of the pro‐inflammatory cytokines, interleukin‐1β and tumor necrosis factor‐α.

the level of the innate immune molecule, surfactant protein‐A (SP‐A), and cytokine levels in vaginal fluid are regulated by the estrous cycle and that the level of SP‐A is positively associated with the level of the pro‐inflammatory cytokine, IL‐8.
the level of the innate host defense molecule, surfactant protein‐A, is regulated by gonadal hormones in the vagina and that this regulation is linked to the regulation of cytokines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the innate immune response in the vagina and the role that this response may play in protecting the host upper genital tract.
the role of the innate immune system in the female reproductive tract, specifically the vagina.
the role of the innate immune system in the vaginal defense against sexually transmitted diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the levels of the innate immune molecule, SP‐A, and cytokines are cyclically regulated in vaginal fluid and that this regulation is dependent on gonadal hormones.
the levels of SP‐A and cytokines are cyclic and that the pattern‐recogniton molecules are regulated by gonadal hormones.

, although the levels of SP‐A, TNFα, IL‐8 and IL‐1β in the human vagina are regulated by gonadal steroids and exhibit cyclic variation during the menstrual cycle, the relationship of the levels of these molecules to each other and their role in the innate immunity of the vagina remains to be determined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a cyclical pattern of surfactant protein‐A and cytokine levels in vaginal fluid, which is consistent with the cyclical pattern of the immune response in other tissues.

the level of the pattern recognition molecule, surfactant protein‐A (SP‐A), is regulated by gonadal hormones, and that SP‐A levels in vaginal fluid are correlated with cytokine levels, particularly interleukin‐1β, which is known to be involved in the recruitment and activation of neutrophils, which are a critical first line of defense against infection in the vagina.

the levels of surfactant protein A, a molecule that is a member of the collection of pattern‐recogniton molecules, is under gonadal hormone control, and that the levels of cytokines in the vagina are also under gonadal hormone influence, and that the cytokines are regulated in a cyclic manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vaginal innate immunity changes cyclically in a pattern that is similar to changes in gonadal hormone levels.

there is an abundance of innate immune molecules in the vaginal fluid, including surfactant protein‐A (SPA), a pattern‐recognition molecule, and cytokines such as interleukin‐8 (IL‐8), IL‐1β, and tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐alpha), in women with and without vaginitis.
the innate host defenses of the vagina are dynamic, and are subject to the influence of both gonadal steroids and cytokines.
